speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
1. With the virtual elimination of diphtheria, whooping cough and smallpox as threats to the nation's health and with the very encouraging progress made in recent

Questions
years in bringing tuberculosis under control, the federal government fully realizes that poliomyelitis has now assumed new prominence as a major public health problem in Canada.
Preliminary figures, with 8,243 cases and a tragic toll of 354 deaths to date, indicate that this year's outbreak of poliomyelitis will prove to be one of the most serious on record.
Assistance under National Health Program
As one means of helping to combat poliomyelitis the federal government has made over $1,500,000 available to the provinces under the national health program.
Of this more than $730,000 has been granted by the federal government to extend research into the value of gamma globulin, to make possible the collection by the Canadian Red Cross Society of large quantities of human blood, and to assist the Connaught laboratories in the increased production of gamma globulin.
The balance has been or is being devoted to such projects as:
Over $177,000 for the purchase of 73 respirators and other technical equipment for the care of poliomyelitis patients in Manitoba.
$159,000 toward the cost of constructing 79 chronic beds and floor area for a health centre in order to establish a polio clinic and health centre at the Victoria public hospital in Fredericton, New Brunswick.
Over $109,000 for the province of Ontario toward the cost of carrying on various investigations and studies relating to poliomyelitis such as:
A study of poliomyelitis during the recovery stages being carried out at the Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto.
An investigation of the antigenic types of poliomyelitis virus prevalent in Canada being carried out in the virus department of the Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto.
An investigation of the role of sewage and water in the spread of poliomyelitis and of improved methods of recovery of poliomyelitis virus from human pathological specimens, carried out at the Connaught medical research laboratories, University of Toronto.
A study of Coxsackie infections in Canada with particular reference to epidemiological features and an investigation of tissue culture techniques as an economical and rapid means of isolating and typing poliomyelitis, being carried out at the Connaught medical research laboratories.
Over $107,000 for the purchase of 56 respirators and other equipment for various

hospitals in Ontario including the Ottawa Civic hospital, Hamilton general hospital, Sault Ste. Marie general hospital, Kingston general hospital, Victoria hospital in London, Port Arthur isolation hospital, Riverdale isolation hospital in Toronto, and for poliomyelitis centres in Kitchener and Sudbury.
Over $71,000 for the province of Quebec toward the cost of carrying on, at the University of Montreal, various research projects relating to poliomyelitis.
Over $46,000 to the province of Alberta to support a free isolation hospital service for poliomyelitis cases paralysed in some degree, and to assist in the care and rehabilitation of adult poliomyelitis cases who developed paralysis prior to the coming into effect of the Alberta polio act of 1938.
Almost $46,000 to the province of Nova Scotia for the payment of a grant to the city of Halifax to compensate it for extending to the province the facilities of the Halifax infectious diseases hospital during a poliomyelitis epidemic, for the purchase of technical equipment and for the employment of professional personnel at the Victoria general hospital, Halifax.
Over $40,000 to the province of British Columbia for the purchase of technical assistance and the employment of special staff including a bracemaker and physiotherapist for the rehabilitation and training of poliomyelitis patients after discharge from hospital.
Over $22,000 to the province of Saskatchewan for the purchase of respirators and other equipment and for the employment of special staff for the Regina cerebral palsy centre for the purpose of the orthopaedic review and supervision of post-polio cases.
Almost $2,500 for the provinces of Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island for the purchase of a hubbard bath and other equipment.
Gamma Globulin
Many questions concerning the use and effectiveness of gamma globulin still remain to be answered. While a great deal of publicity has been given to its value in modifying the paralysis which may follow an attack of poliomyelitis, the use of this blood fraction is still in the experimental stage.
Interest in Canada in the use of gamma globulin for preventing or lessening the severity of paralysis from poliomyelitis was increased by reports of trials made in the United States. In Cleveland last year at the meeting of the American public health association Dr. W. McD. Hammon of Pittsburgh reported the results of tests involving some 55,000 children. Dr. Hammon found among

that half of the experimental group which received gamma globulin injections an encouraging decrease in paralytic poliomyelitis cases as well as a significant modification in the severity of the paralysis in those who contracted the disease.
In view of this evidence, inconclusive as it may have been, a conference was called in Ottawa last January under the chairmanship of my deputy minister of health, Dr. G. D. W. Cameron, to consider all aspects of the problem. The public health and research experts attending this conference agreed that, while final judgment should be reserved until more facts were known, every effort should be made to increase the supply of gamma globulin.
Fortunately, the Connaught medical research laboratories in Toronto not only had scientific personnel familiar with the complex processes involved in the production of gamma globulin but had a supply of blood serum on hand which had been stored from the second world war. With funds provided out of the national health program, special production facilities were set up and the Connaught laboratories worked night and day to produce the needed supplies of gamma globulin.
The truly remarkable results achieved in producing approximately 25,000 average doses of gamma globulin is a tribute to Dr. R. D. Defries and his staff at the Connaught medical research laboratories.
To ensure that the limited quantities of the serum would be used to the very best advantage, an advisory committee representing federal and provincial health departments and university medical research centres was set up to assist in the distribution of gamma globulin. It was agreed that supplies would be made available only through provincial health departments and that allocations would be made by the committee to those areas where poliomyelitis reached epidemic proportions. The serum was reserved for administration to those in the younger age group who had been directly exposed to paralytic poliomyelitis.
In view of the severity of the epidemic in Manitoba, additional supplies of gamma globulin were earmarked for that province permitting public health officials to provide injections to persons under 30 coming in contact with paralytic cases as well as to voluntary nurses working in poliomyelitis wards.
That it has been possible to meet all requests for gamma globulin this summer and fall is a tribute to the work of Dr. Milton Brown and the members of the advisory
Questions
committee and to Dr. B. D. B. Layton of the Department of National Health and Welfare who had responsibility for the day to day administration of the committee's distribution policy. It is also a high tribute to the understanding and restraint exhibited by the provincial health departments in assessing local situations and presenting their requests to the committee.
An important feature of the program was the recommendation made by the committee that follow-up studies should be conducted where gamma globulin had been administered. It was suggested that information should be gathered, wherever possible, by a team consisting of a health officer and public health nurses. From a research standpoint, the value of this procedure is inestimable and it is expected that the reports of these teams will provide valuable information on which further studies of the effectiveness of the serum can be made.
Plans have just been completed with the provincial health authorities to undertake an expanded program next year under which the facilities of the Connaught laboratories will be increased so that production can be more than doubled. $270,000 is being provided under the national health program for this purpose this year. In addition, almost $315,000 is being made available this year under the national health program to make it possible for the Canadian Red Cross Society to collect the large quantities of human blood needed for this greatly increased production of gamma globulin. It is hoped that the importance of the gamma globulin program will give new incentive to the public to donate their blood and to lend their financial support to the vital work of the Canadian Red Cross.
While gamma globulin, in the light of present knowledge, is the most effective weapon in the fight against poliomyelitis, it should be remembered that it only provides a degree of protection for a limited time-perhaps five weeks at best. This "passive immunization" has not in the past proved entirely satisfactory for the control of other infectious diseases and will almost certainly be replaced when a more lasting immunizing agent for poliomyelitis is developed. The final answer to the control of poliomyelitis will be found in the production of a vaccine that will confer a lasting immunity.
Important progress has already been made in this direction and federal aid is now being given to research studies at the Toronto hospital for sick children and the school of hygiene at the University of Montreal. The Toronto research, which is being directed by Dr. A. J. Rhodes, has been undertaken to

Questions
investigate more thoroughly than has previously been possible the various strains of the poliomyelitis virus in Canada and to And out which of the three common types cause poliomyelitis epidemics in this country.
This project is being correlated with work on the development of a poliomyelitis vaccine which Dr. Rhodes is carrying forward at the Connaught laboratories. In this connection, it was recently announced that progress had been made in producing poliomyelitis virus in quantity-a necessary and important step in the production of any poliomyelitis vaccine.
Special Assistance
Finally, special assistance has been provided to the provinces by medical officers of the epidemiology division of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Throughout last spring that division secured from the United States public health service the latest information on the use of gamma globulin and distributed it to the provincial health departments. In this way the provinces were kept fully informed of current knowledge regarding the prevention of poliomyelitis and the use of gamma globulin.
This year, starting on May 1 instead of on July 1 as is usual, weekly telegraphic reports were procured from the provincial health departments of the weekly incidence of poliomyelitis. This data was used not only to keep the federal department fully informed of the situation throughout Canada but to assist the advisory committee in the distribution of gamma globulin to particularly acute areas.
With regard to Manitoba: as the incidence of poliomyelitis had gained unusual momentum by the middle of July, the Manitoba health department asked that Dr. A. F. W. Peart, chief of the epidemiology division of the Department of National Health and Welfare, go to Winnipeg for consultation. Dr. Peart arrived in Winnipeg on July 21. He reviewed the various control procedures that were being carried out in the isolation of cases, the quarantine of contact procedures regarding camps and schools, milk and water supplies and discussed the use of gamma globulin. Special provisions were made, including arrangements to enable nurses and other hospital attendants in the poliomyelitis hospital and their children to receive protective injections of gamma globulin. All paralytic poliomyelitis patients, whether they received gamma globulin or not, were followed up as a research project of the advisory committee.
On August 14 the Manitoba health department asked Dr. Peart to return to Winnipeg to consult with the local poliomyelitis committee. By this time the weekly incidence had reached more than 200 cases. Again Dr. Peart reviewed what was already being done and supported the provincial health department in connection with the various procedures that were being carried out.
To summarize, the federal government is keeping very closely in touch with this serious situation and is co-operating wholeheartedly with the provinces in providing substantial assistance and support.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: ALLEGED ABUSE OF MEMBERS' FRANKING PRIVILEGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Acting Postmaster General. Some days ago the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite) asked a question with regard to franking privileges. As this is a matter of concern to all hon. members I think we should know where we stand as to whether any report has been made or will be made in answer to the point raised by the hon. member for Skeena.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Acting Posfmaster General):
maintopic: ALLEGED ABUSE OF MEMBERS' FRANKING PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
Some days ago I addressed a letter on this subject to the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), and I think the simplest way to answer the hon. gentleman's question is to read that letter to the house. It is dated November 23, 1953, and reads:
Dear Mr. Blackmore,
On Thursday last, November 19th, Mr. Applewhaite asked me, in the House of Commons, about the apparent abuse of members' franking privileges as reported in the Ottawa Journal of November 18th.
In reply, I stated that the item in the Journal was a reprint from the Calgary Herald, and that I had asked the Post Office Department to communicate with the editor of the Calgary Herald to see whether we could get both the cover and the contents, so we could find out which member's frank had been used. I added that I assumed, from the article, that the frank had been used improperly. By improperly I meant without the knowledge of the member concerned.
The Post Office Department has now received from the editor of the Calgary Herald an envelope which bears your frank, and which contained a copy of the American Mercury for September, 1953, containing an article, to which attention was drawn, entitled "The Truth about Joe McCarthy". The envelope also contained advertisements for a book entitled "The Iron Curtain Over America" by John Beaty, and another book "While You Slept: Our Tragedy in Asia and Who Made It" by John T. Flynn. A note was enclosed, dated from Wood-roffe post office, November 4th, and bearing the signature of Doris A. Moore.
There seems to be no question that this is mailable matter under section 17 of the Post Office Act, which the post office has an obligation to transmit free of postage when sent by a member of the Senate or the House of Commons at Ottawa during a session of parliament or during the ten days immediately preceding or following a session of

parliament, and it is postmarked November 5th, which was only seven days before parliament met. Consequently, the only question which arises so far as the Post Office Department is concerned, is whether this material was posted on your behalf or with your authority. I am accordingly enclosing the envelope and contents received from the Calgary Herald, so that you may take whatever action, if any, you consider to be required in the circumstances.
That I signed as Acting Postmaster General.

maintopic: ALLEGED ABUSE OF MEMBERS' FRANKING PRIVILEGES
speechtext: The point is, it was mailable matter.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, December 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. A. H. Hollingworth for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Low.
(Translation):

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am greatly honoured to be able to take part in the debate on the address in

reply to the speech from the throne after receiving a second mandate from the electors of my constituency.
I owe the honour and satisfaction of coming back to the house to the good administration of the Liberal party, which I have supported loyally during the four years I have been a member of the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, it affords me great pleasure to congratulate you on your election to the office you now hold and which, I am sure, will give you the opportunity of making friends on both sides of the house. Knowing your loyalty and fairness, everyone will be happy at the wise and sound decisions you will be called upon to make.
I avail myself of this opportunity to offer my congratulations and best wishes to the new ministers, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) and the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Lesage). The latter will have to take a paternal attitude towards his eastern neighbour, because my constituents see in him a guiding beacon for our youth.
I must also congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Hollingworth and Mr. Villeneuve). On that occasion, they loyally served the interests of their constituents. The honour which was theirs on that occasion is shared by the citizens who showed confidence in them.
Now I wish to thank those who placed their confidence in me during the last electoral campaign. I cannot shirk from fulfilling the task my constituents have given me, that of presenting to the house their claims, their wishes, and their aspirations. If I cannot match their lofty sentiments, I shall try at least to show myself worthy of the consideration I have received from them.
During my last electoral campaign, I deemed it my duty to respect the opinions, good or bad, of my opponents, reserving myself the right of expressing my own, and I am sure that the success I have had in that campaign is due to my esteem and consideration for the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent), which are widely shared by my constituents.
I am not one of those who believe that the government of a country cannot withstand criticism, because there will always be improvements to be made in order to keep up with the speedy evolution of our times. However, I am convinced that our government
The Address-Mr. Masse does its best to bring every citizen of Canada the maximum of happiness and prosperity.
There is always some ideal which we never attain. As soon as we realize part of our program, we discover new horizons. Our workers always fear the possibility of sickness, unemployment, or accidents, but the government cannot solve all those problems overnight. However, it is the duty of the government to present measures of such a nature as to stimulate production, encourage initiative, and raise the standards 'of living of our people, in such a way as to bring some measure of welfare and happiness to our society. In that respect, the Liberal government has for many years fulfilled that duty.
There is no need today to give a topographical and geographical description of my riding; I have already had the occasion of doing so here in this house.
The county of Kamouraska comprises 679,040 acres, 76 per cent of which is covered with forest; the cultivated area represents 22 per cent of the total area, thus 98 per cent of the whole area is considered as productive. Only 2 per cent of the area is unproductive, and this includes roads, lakes and rivers.
Agriculture is consequently our chief industry and our farmers are not satisfied with the prices which they have been getting for their products, compared with the prices paid by the consumer. Agriculture, in that part of the country, is a family undertaking and according to tradition, a son succeeds his father on the family homestead and then hands it over to his own son after having tilled it successfully.
I have received a request from the president of the farmers' union of the parish of Ste. Perpetue, in the county of L'lslet, telling me that the farmers of that village want assistance for the drainage of land and the removal of rocks. Such a matter falls within the jurisdiction of the provincial government; however, I am of the opinion that there should be some co-operation between the central government and the provinces. There are problems the solution of which involves an expenditure of money beyond the means of our farmers, on account of the high cost of those services.
I must thank the right hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for the establishment and rapid improvement of the experimental farm at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere. Experimentation and research are, first and foremost, a government responsibility and must be carried out in every
550	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Masse possible field. We must not forget that farmers work hard from dawn to dusk and are in no position to carry out research because of the size of their farms and their present low level of income. They are convinced that the cost of living will not be lowered by reduced hours of work or increased wages, but rather by the generous co-operation of all classes that make up the Canadian nation.
As far as the experimental farm at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere is concerned, I think it would be wise to carry out reforestation and make tree plots out of the uncultivated portions. In the county of Kamouraska the forest is the necessary complement to agriculture. Without parallel development of land and forest there is a danger of upsetting the economy of my constituency.
Ever since I have been sitting in this house, I have asked year after year that protecting walls be erected, among other places, in the parish of Riviere Ouelle, in order to protect certain properties which will be destroyed in the very near future, at the present rate of erosion. If this situation is not remedied now, much of the land in this cove will vanish.
Mr. Speaker, allow me to inform you of the contents of a resolution which was prepared in 1952, and again in 1953, by the local section, in my county, of the "Union Catholique des Cultivateurs". This resolution called, first, for the appointment of a representative to the Vatican and, second, for the adoption of a Canadian flag. I have already given my approval here to these two resolutions.
Moreover, 1 should be very pleased were the central government to co-operate with provincial authorities, in order to solve problems of interest to the community at large. I am not one of those who believe that the government of a country is perfect, but I am convinced that the government headed by the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent has given the nation a development and impetus which cannot be stopped. All classes of society, and especially the social outcasts and the disabled, must have seen a ray of sunshine when they read in the speech from the throne that the state would come to their assistance.
In the field of international relations, it seems to me that the different nations should act toward each other in a more charitable manner; in this respect Canada has largely done its share. The free world is forced to set up an international police force, so that each nation will be able to count on a larger measure of security. When I hear state-


ments to the effect that we are too generous towards other peoples, I can do no better than quote an editorial written by Gerard Filion and published in Le Devoir on November 14, 1953:
Communism has no need to hurry, tor it knows that time is on its side. It aspires to conquer the world less through force than through ideas. Communism is the new messianism. It promises its followers the advent of an earthly paradise, founded on human equality and fraternity. What does it matter if facts are inconsistent with principles in the nations where communism reigns supreme? Men are more attached to ideas which flatter them, than to facts which rebuke them. Communism is an opiate for all those who live it through the prism of their imagination. And communism is reckoning with this very attraction in its quest for world mastery. Poverty is its main ally. And poverty is rampant in our present world.
I think it is only wise to use our surplus agricultural products to feed the hungry, so as to make friends of starving populations.
Our farmers are somewhat worried by the falling prices of beef and potatoes. However, they trust that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who has so ably administered his department under circumstances which were sometimes difficult, will be able to find a constructive way to solve these recurring problems.
Allow me to avail myself of this opportunity to point out to the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) that some wharves in my county are urgently in need of repairs, if they are to serve the purpose for which they were built. In Kamouraska, it is essential that wharves be in good condition because the river-used to transport pulpwood by ship-and our roads are the only two channels of communication through which we can ship and receive industrial goods.
In these troubled times, I believe we should lay special stress on charity and understanding among all classes of society. Was it not the Pope, the head of Christianity, who asked the peoples of the world to work more closely together so that modern achievements may serve constructive and not destructive purposes.
Mr. Speaker, I have made these few remarks in the hope of serving the nation at large and my electors in particular.

May I have the honour, Mr. Speaker, of offering my most sincere congratulations to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on the dignity with which he conducted his last electoral campaign. All the population of Kamouraska is grateful to him, and as long as the Liberal party goes forward on the

route which it has taken, and in which he has directed it, the future of our country, Canada, will be safe.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to concur wholeheartedly in the many sincere congratulations which have been extended to you and all others who have received promotions since the last parliament. I also congratulate the members who were elected in August last. I am sorry of course that there are not more on this side of the house. However, we still have great hopes that time and the interests of Canada will correct this serious fault. It is good to note, as has been expressed here a number of times, the many young members who were elected at the last election. This of course is as it should be. It keeps parliament forever young and forever hopeful, as was so well expressed in an editorial in the Ottawa Journal a short time ago.
Most of the problems that face the people of Canada and this parliament today are the same problems we have had for the last ten years or more. First in importance of course is the matter of defence. This has already been mentioned by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). The information he gave the house was very limited and leaves a wide opportunity for him to discuss this matter further during the session. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) referred to the dearth of information when he spoke a few days ago. We all agree that it is still necessary, and we fear will be necessary for some time, to spend enormous amounts of money in the defence of our country. Our object of course is to see that it is spent wisely and not wasted.
Another serious problem is the question of housing which was dealt with a few days ago in a speech by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). We were very pleased to hear that 100,000 units will probably be built during the coming year. This of course still leaves much to be desired. I understand that the need of housing in Canada today runs well over half a million, and I also understand that so far as veterans housing is concerned about 250,000 houses are still needed for our veterans.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce also mentioned the matter of markets when he spoke a few days ago. He claimed that we in the opposition were very pessimistic regarding the market situation. This may be true. However, if we are pessimistic there is good reason and there are many others who agree with us, because I am sure if the minister questioned the farmers of the country he would find that they also feel that there is room for pessimism. The manufacturers of textiles are also very pessimistic
The Address-Mr. Brooks with respect to their situation. So also are the machinery manufacturers. I know that lumber operators in my part of Canada, and I am sure in other parts of Canada too, are wondering where their future markets will be.
As the minister said, we may be pessimistic but it does occur to me that sometimes people can be too optimistic in the same way that they can be too pessimistic, and I think at this time possibly the minister is too optimistic. The debate on the throne speech has now been under way for a long time. Many hon. members have taken the opportunity of speaking and it has been a great pleasure to me, as one of the older members of the house, to listen to the many excellent speeches that have been delivered by younger members, especially those who have come to the house for the first time.
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) said in his speech yesterday that I was to be congratulated in that I was not surrounded as he is by a minister and two parliamentary assistants. We in New Brunswick do not quite feel that way. We would like to have our full share of ministers and parliamentary assistants. While there are two parliamentary assistants from Nova Scotia there are none from New Brunswick. With the support that the province of New Brunswick has given the government we believe that there might well be a parliamentary assistant from that province. I know there are a number of members on the government side who feel they are well qualified indeed for that position.
If we have a complaint in New Brunswick, it would seem that the people of Newfoundland have a greater complaint. While there is a minister elected from the province of Newfoundland, still he is not a native of that province, and it did seem to me and I am sure it must have occurred to many in the house, particularly to members from Newfoundland, that one of their number might very well have been chosen to present the problems of their province because no one understands the problems of a province as well as a man who is born and brought up there.
My chief object in speaking this afternoon is to deal with a matter which concerns my own constituency in particular, although it is of some concern to the whole of Canada as well. Hon. members will recall that during last year the Minister of National Defence announced that a large military camp would be established in New Brunswick. This camp, as all will remember, was established partly in my constituency and partly in the constituency of York-Sunbury. I have discussed this matter quite extensively already in this
552	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Brooks house and have expressed my views. I said that while we were pleased that the camp was being located in New Brunswick, we felt that some other sections of the province could have been chosen. I am not going to tire the house with the arguments I used at that time. It is an accomplished fact now that this camp is established in the Gagetown area, and nothing I could say would change it.
But I will say this, Mr. Speaker, that the people in this area, who were given very little warning that their properties would be taken over for a military camp, were stunned when they found they would have to leave the section of the country in which their ancestors had lived for a great many years. Just a few weeks before coming to Ottawa I visited this section, and it is a sad sight to see the vacant farms. It is a sad sight to see one vacant farm, to see the house with weeds growing up around it, to see the vacant windows and perhaps the barn doors off their hinges. However, when you go through a whole countryside and see house after house closed up, the barns closed, the grass growing around the houses; when you see the vacant churches, the vacant halls and the vacant schools, to me at least it is a sad sight indeed. As I say, the matter has been dealt with and settled by the government, so there is not much purpose in my mentioning it to any extent today.
These people who have moved out of this area have, for the most part, gone to other parts of New Brunswick. Many of them have settled in my own locality in and around the town of Sussex and the Kennebecasis valley. They are admirable people and have been welcomed in every community in which they have settled. Already they are taking an active part in the activities of their new communities. There is another class of people that was greatly affected by the selection of this campsite, and that is the people on the fringe of the campsite between the Gagetown camp area and the Saint John river. In this area there is a fringe about a mile wide in some places and two or three miles in others. This section is still quite thickly settled. There are fine farms and lovely villages in this section. Today these people are wondering just what their situation is.
The back country, as they call the area from which these farmers have been moved, supplied the merchants with trade and the mills with lumber as well as the dairies with milk for the manufacture of cheese and butter. In the village of Hampstead, for instance, there was a dairy which has been closed because 75 per cent of the milk supplied to it came from this back area. At Gagetown there is a lumber mill belonging to the firm of Reid Brothers, in addition to other
fMr. Brooks.]

lumber mills, and this back area supplied those mills with the round lumber with which to carry on their operations. No doubt the mill will close, with the result that many people will be out of work. The storekeepers in the area tell me that over 50 per cent of their trade is gone. Men who were selling farm machinery say that they have lost over 75 per cent of their trade. The whole of this 20-mile strip along the Saint John river between the boundary of the military campsite and the river is in a bad way today.
There are some very fine villages in that section, as I am sure my good friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) could tell you. There are no more beautiful villages in the whole of New Brunswick, perhaps even in Canada, than Gagetown, Hampstead, and Welsford. A request was made of the government that these small places be given more consideration, but the larger places like Fredericton and Saint John, which evidently have more pull, are getting the benefits. So far as I can gather, these places which have really suffered from the establishment of the camp are not receiving the consideration they should receive. This area should receive first consideration, and it should receive consideration before Saint John or Fredericton. Neither of these cities has lost anything as a result of the camp being moved into this area, but the other section has lost a great deal.
There is also the matter of labour. The labouring men in this area have lost their employment in the mills and other places; and though the department has promised to give them first consideration-and I believe the Minister of Labour and those higher up in the province of New Brunswick are willing that this should be done-I know of cases in which the men are not receiving the consideration promised. They claim that the reason for this, and 1 think there is considerable truth in it, is that they do not belong to the right provincial party. I hope that this matter will receive careful consideration. I know that it is sometimes difficult to control some of the local politicians, but that is exactly what should and must be done so far as this area is concerned.
The county of Queens itself, Mr. Speaker, has also sustained great loss. The three parishes of Hampstead, Gagetown and Peters-ville, which have been affected, were three of the outstanding parishes in the county. The parish of Petersville is practically all gone, while the parishes of Hampstead and Gagetown have been cut in two. These parishes still have their burdens to bear as parishes. In making up assessments to carry on public services, the county of Queens will sustain a loss of revenue. I hope that if the

government has not made arrangements to suitably compensate this county they will do so in generous terms.
Speaking of what might be done for these places like Gagetown and Hampstead and other places along the river, I suggest that the government no doubt will build a number of residences for married quarters. I do not know of any finer place where quarters for married people or other quarters could be constructed than right at the village of Gagetown, one of the oldest villages in New Brunswick, first settled by the French many years ago, later by the British, followed by the United Empire Loyalists. It is one of the most historic villages in New Brunswick.
There is the question of the location of hospitals. In a large military establishment of this kind there are bound to be a number of hospitals required, and it seems to me this would be the ideal spot for the location of a hospital or hospitals. Workshops could be established there, and recreation centres. I hope that the Department of National Defence will carefully consider the sacrifices which have been made by the people in this area and the possibility that the future economy of this section will be greatly affected, and that they will give every consideration to the people and the industries alike along what I call this fringe area.
Another matter is giving the people of this area some concern. Very often outside the camp area engineers and others from the Department of National Defence are seen making surveys here and there. These people are afraid that some day they will be told, as were the people in the area itself, that they will have to give up their properties and move out. Their minds should be set at rest in that regard as soon as possible. Even across the Saint John river in the vicinity of Cambridge, surveys have been made not only by military officers from our own department but also by United States officers, and people over there are alarmed. They fear that some of their properties are to be taken away. As I say, this fear should be allayed as quickly as possible. I have nothing more to say in that connection. I do think a great debt is owing to the people in this area, one that I hope the department will make every effort to pay.
I come to another matter that is very important to us and that has already been discussed by some of the previous speakers from New Brunswick. I may say it has been dealt with many many times by members who have been here in the past. I refer to the hydro development in our province. In the 18 years I have been in the house this matter has been brought up 83276-36
The Address-Mr. Brooks time and time again, and all the hydroelectric prospects which have been mentioned here recently have been mentioned before; it is an old story, and I am not surprised that it is being mentioned again, because like many old stories nothing has been done about it and we are in much the same position as we have been in the past.
I am told that the per capita horsepower in the Dominion of Canada is one; that is, about 14 million horsepower for the whole dominion. We have nearly 500,000 people in New Brunswick and our horsepower amounts to 141,000 for the whole province. With the large military camp coming to our province there will be a much greater need for electric power. We need more so far as our domestic consumption is concerned, but most of all today we need power for the development of our natural resources.
We have been known in the past as a province which had very little mineral resources. Very extensive mineral deposits have recently been found in New Brunswick, and we believe that with the proper development of those mineral deposits the economy and the future of our province can be greatly enhanced.
I should like to read part of an article which appeared in the Toronto Telegram. This is the opinion of Mr. M. J. Boylen, head of several mining companies in Ontario. He had this to say:
Recent mineral discoveries in the province-
He was speaking of New Brunswick.
-have attracted widespread attention, and Mr. Boylen estimates that its deposits of lead, zinc, silver and iron ore may be the largest in North America. That is taking in a lot of territory, but at any rate these minerals are likely to become the basis of a big chemical industry.
I mention these things simply to show the great need of electric power in the province of New Brunswick.
A few days ago an hon. member mentioned 'Quoddy. Older members in the house have heard 'Quoddy mentioned many times. It is an old story. Over 25 years ago, when I was a member of the local legislature at Fredericton, a Mr. Cooper from the United States came to Fredericton and tried to interest the province of New Brunswick in a joint development of the Passamaquoddy, and he certainly told us a very interesting story. He presented a model of the dams and so on that might be used in 'Quoddy, and told us about the great surge of the tides that we all knew. He spoke of their rise of 40 feet, and illustrated to us the enormous power potentiality in the tides in the Passamaquoddy.
The international joint commission investigated this hydro prospect a few years ago, and while they did not altogether claim
554	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Brooks that it was feasible they said that further investigation should be made, and they estimated that the cost would be $3,900,000. This cost would be borne jointly by the United States and Canada. They recommended that investigations be made. I believe the United States is prepared to go ahead with the investigation and pay its share, but the attitude of the Canadian government is one of indifference. I again urge the government, as I did last year, to join with the United States and make this necessary investigation.
I could go on and mention some of the other prospects that have been mentioned, such as the Chignecto. Everyone is acquainted with the Chignecto. My old seatmate, Percy Black, who sat with me for years-and, may I interject, I do not think any finer gentleman has ever sat in the House of Commons since I came here-was a strong advocate and champion of the Chignecto. I myself believe that if a canal was constructed on the Chignecto it would be a great boon to shipping in the maritime provinces, and also extensive hydroelectric power could be developed. I remember that a few years ago a delegation from the city of Saint John and from other parts of the maritime provinces came to Ottawa to interview the government in this connection. While they were treated very courteously-I attended the meeting-if ever a delegation got a brush-off I am satisfied that this delegation got a decided one. It was very discouraging from the point of view of both these projects, shipping and electric power.
Then we had the Petitcodiac. The former member for Westmorland brought this up in the house and urged an investigation into the Petitcodiac possibility. The engineers did not report favourably on the Petitcodiac because of the soft bottom of the river, and so on, which made it practically impossible to construct storage dams.
However, there is another project receiving more attention now, one which I hope will not have the same fate as the Quoddy, the Chignecto and the Petitcodiac-I refer to the Saint John river development. As hon. members know, the Saint John river is the second largest river on the eastern coast of the North American continent. It is 450 miles long from its source to the sea, its tributaries rising in Quebec and the state of Maine.
Some years ago a development on the Saint John was completed at Grand Falls and there is now a smaller development on the Tobique. I am informed that if storage dams were constructed on the Saint John river, its tributaries and lakes, 250,000 horsepower could be developed. The provincial government


has been negotiating with the state of Maine and the province of Quebec. I understand the state of Maine has taken a kindly view of the matter as more power is required in the upper part of ithat state.
Unfortunately certain sections of the province of Quebec feel that injury will be done to farmlands in the vicinity of Lake Temis-couata and other sections. The hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Legare) said in the house the other day that he hoped something would be done to prevent New Brunswick going ahead with the proposed development of the Saint John river. I remember that last year the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) expressed the hope that nothing would be done.
I have discussed this matter with some of the government officials in New Brunswick and with the engineers and they tell me that in their opinion the fears of the people in those sections of Quebec are not justified. I do hope that nothing will be done to prevent the future development of this great waterway. The full development would mean that power would be generated at Beechwood and Macnaquac and more at Grand Falls.
I think it was the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) who referred a few days ago to Grand Falls and said that that development had been given away by the Conservative party in 1926 or 1927. That is an old story down in that province. It is an old election battlecry. It is even older than the prediction that if the Tories come into power they will do away with old age pensions and children's allowances, and there is just about as much truth in it.
The development at Grand Falls has been the main source of power in New Brunswick. The industrial development at Dalhousie, Edmundston and other parts of New Brunswick and the development of our pulp and paper industry is due to the power development at Grand Falls. I do not think the people in those towns and the thousands of men who work in the woods will say the development at Grand Falls, even though it was by private capital, was a mistake. It has been of great help to our province and I hope more private capital will come into the province to develop other water power sites.
I was pleased to note by the speech from the throne that consideration is to be given this year to disabled persons. I think most hon. members at some time or other have indicated that this class of our citizens should receive consideration. As I say, I am pleased that it is mentioned in the speech from the

throne. I can assure you that when the legislation comes before the house it will have my full support.
There is just one comment I should like to make in this connection. I remember that when the Old Age Pensions Act was passed by the federal government the provincial governments were asked to contribute 50 per cent of the cost. At that time many of the poorer provinces were not able to make their contribution, with the result that the people in some of the richer provinces of Canada received their old age pensions some years before those in the poorer provinces. I should like to see the federal government assume full responsibility for the payment of pensions to totally disabled persons. I feel that, like pensions for the blind, this is a federal government responsibility.
Our province was one of the last to give pensions to our older people. It was not because we did not want to; we just could not afford to do it, or at least it was felt that we could not afford it. I am quite certain that the provincial government of New Brunswick will do its part as far as providing pensions for disabled persons is concerned, but in order to make sure that all people of this class in Canada receive what I feel they are entitled to, it should be made a federal responsibility.
We are considered to be a have-not province, and in this connection I should like to quote from an editorial which appeared recently in one of the newspapers. It reads:
The Toronto Globe and Mail develops a thesis that the less prosperous provinces are partly to blame for their own troubles in that they have come to Ottawa asking for "doles, not development."
The editorial then goes on to quote part of the editorial which had appeared in the Globe and Mail:
If, says the Globe and Mail, half the money spent during recent years to prop up the economies of these provinces had been used to build up their economies instead, there would be no talk of 'haves' and 'have-nots'. All would be 'haves'.
It is all very well for the Toronto Globe and Mail to lecture us in that regard, but the fact is that we have received no more or perhaps even less than some of those provinces which are called the "have" provinces. While this is an old story and some may smile, I should like to point out to the house that the maritime provinces have contributed, both in materials and in people, perhaps more than any other section of Canada to the building up of the larger and western provinces.
Then again, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick were two of the four provinces which 83276-36i
The Address-Mr. Brooks first formed this dominion. We were a province long before the days of confederation. The great public domain in this country was purchased by money from the other provinces of Canada. We in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island helped to pay for all this great domain which was afterwards given to Alberta and Saskatchewan, to Ontario and to Quebec, and even Newfoundland today has a section. Our provinces, circumscribed as they are by the sea, could not in any way benefit by this great extension in the northern part of our dominion. While we helped to pay for it, while we helped to develop it, and while we helped to defend it, we obtained no benefit from this great development in the other parts of Canada.
We all know what the northern lands mean to these provinces with their oil and their minerals and other great resources, but we have received no benefit as far as these things are concerned.

That is a long, long story and I do not think I would be justified in taking up the time of the house in dealing with it at present. I am just mentioning these things. I am not telling the government what they should do, but in justice to the maritimes I think I should tell them what the situation is; then they themselves would be in a position to do what is necessary.
In closing, I want to touch briefly on veterans affairs. In the 18 years I have been in the House of Commons I have been a member of every veterans affairs committee. I have admired the different veterans organizations in Canada for their fairness and their strong advocacy of what they consider the rights of the veterans. I have seen the Legion's brief which was presented to the government a short time ago, and in general I agree with practically everything in that brief. I would like to see also, as I and many other hon. members have advocated, a veterans affairs committee set up at this session of parliament where this brief submitted by the veterans might be very carefully considered, because after all I think it is in a veterans affairs committee that justice can best be done to veterans. You hear their problems and you also hear from officers of the Department of Veterans Affairs, and between the two the committee can decide what is best and what can be done in the matter of veterans legislation.

The Address-Mr. A. Stewart

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak about the national film board. I realize I am in a somewhat vulnerable position, because I should have said what I am going to say last session when the estimates were before the house. That I did not do so was entirely my own fault and I accept responsibility for it, although I cannot help wishing that the government would refrain from bringing down controversial legislation or even estimates in the dying hours of the session.
Before I deal with the present situation I should like to refresh the minds of hon. members on the recent history of the national film board. I want to go back to 1939 when the National Film Act was passed and the purpose of the film board as read into that act was:
To help Canadians in all parts of Canada to understand the ways of living and the problems of Canadians in other parts-
And furthermore, of course-
-to take care of the distribution of films in other countries.
To take charge of the film board the government had the wisdom to appoint a very able young man, John Grierson, who had already made a reputation for himself in the United Kingdom with documentary films. Mr. Grierson rapidly built around himself a capable and brilliant group of aides. Grierson had been accustomed in the United Kingdom to working in the same way that he ultimately worked here, that is with a government agency and with the help of small private companies. Certainly there was never at any time any attempt to make the film board a monopoly. That was one of the charges in the attacks made against the film board by, of course, the Conservative party. The film board was never a monopoly and it is not so today. It was the film board which helped build that very well known Ottawa firm which owes a great deal to the film board for the position which it has now reached today. I refer, of course, to Crawley Films.
The board got to work, yet even before it started the attacks were obvious. They started before birth, continued after birth and during adolescence, an adolescence which was amazingly mature, and these attacks are still apparent today coming principally from groups such as chambers of commerce. Mr. Grierson gathered round him a group of very able younger people to start the film board. Some were British and some American, but quickly young Canadians began to join the film board, Canadians with artistic sensibility and with creative capacity. They were primarily, I suppose, individualists and nonconformists. It was much more popular in
(Mr. Brooks.]
those days to be non-conformist than in some places it is today, but then I have never been able to see how the film board could get very far without being non-conformist.
The board gave these young men and women an opportunity to display their talents, an opportunity which was denied them by private industry in this country. They were young men and women who believed in Canada and they had a vision. They wanted to show the rest of the people of this country what that vision was and their medium was on film. They did a wonderfully successful job, not only in the eyes of Canadians but in the view of people all over the world.
Of course, with the outbreak of war there was a tremendous impetus given to the film board and the government had the good sense to realize that the board could be more than useful. Let me read an interesting quotation from the Financial Post dated September 6, 1941, which said, dealing with the national film board:
Behind all this activity is a theory that the film is a social instrument to help the citizen understand, by visual means, the complex workings of modern administration and industry. The drama of machines is stressed. There flashes across the screen an impressive panorama of the manifold jobs that go to make up our armament and military effort. There are no studio actors. They are not needed. The men and women themselves, filmed at work, provide the talent; they give true realism to the action.
And of course the same is true of the board today. As the Financial Post said, and some persons regret now, the film was "a social instrument", and was used accordingly.
The film board expanded rapidly during these years of war and even more rapidly in the days of peace following because the people of Canada realized what the national film board had come to mean to them. They wanted this expansion because they appreciated its work. In 1949 there were about 250 film councils and about the same number of film libraries and there were at least 3,000 outlets for 16 mm. film and the surprising number of one million people per month saw these films. One can see easily the important part this agency played in the life of Canadians. It was regarded by other countries as being an important medium too, for many construed it as a model which should be followed in their own countries and they studied and copied it with some care.
I think the secret of the film board's success then was that the board was regarded as a creative agency, and not just an administrative agency.

But during all these years the attacks against it were mounting, and of course they rose to a crescendo in 1949. The pity of it is that the film board got no support from those from whom they should expect it, namely from the government itself. Indeed, there were members of the cabinet who went out of their way in this house to say things about the film board that were demonstrably not in accordance with the facts. One of these gentlemen was the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and the other, unfortunately, was the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent).
Naturally when these two gentlemen made the statements they did in the house it was grist to the mill of the private enterprisers, and they climbed on the loyalty bandwagon. The personnel of the film board were screened. Screening was very popular back in 1949. It got to the stage where fiddle players at the C.B.C. were being screened for loyalty tests. I hope we have gotten over that sort of hysteria. But we had the unfortunate spectacle here in parliament of the film board, which made a presentation to the Massey commission, being partly disavowed by the minister who was then in charge of the board. Had I been a member of the organization in those days I think my motto would have been "Heaven preserve me from my friends".
The attack on the loyalty of the individuals was continued. It was a marvellous stick with which to beat this agency which the private film interests did not like at all. Those private film interests were very powerful. There is no question in my mind that they were inspired from Hollywood. The chambers of commerce in Canada of course took up the cry. In 1949 there was a convention of Canadian chambers of commerce in Montreal. There a resolution was passed charging the board with having created a monopoly in films in this country and asking the government to eliminate unfair competition between the agency and private producers.
When one examines the parentage of the resolution it is rather interesting to note that there were two separate motions before the chambers of commerce. One came from General Films of Regina and the other came from a professional firm in the city, Arthur A. Crawley and Company. Perhaps it is just coincidence-I do not know; I doubt it- that the son of Mr. Arthur A. Crawley happens to be the F. R. Crawley who is the head of Crawley Films in this city, a company which was built up in no small measure owing to what the film board did. The net result of all this was that the government
The Address-Mr. A. Stewart bowed to the phony and synthetic attacks; they bowed by getting rid of the then commissioner in a rather extraordinary way, and of course appointing another in his stead.
We were told that the change in commissioners was in order to restore public confidence in the film board. I never knew for a moment that there was any lack of public confidence in the film board. What there was, of course, was lack on the part of the government of any policy concerning the film board, or of any desire indeed to protect it. This is what the public of that day had to say about the film board. The Canadian federation of home and school said:
Canadians need films that can be supplied by the N.F.B. better than any other producer.
The Canadian association for adult education said:
C.A.A.E. expresses its appreciation and approval, in principle, of the important contribution to public information and understanding made by the government of Canada through the agency of the N.F.B.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture said:
The program of the N.F.B. has been of very great value to rural people. It has met the need in thousands of rural district which has undoubtedly enriched the life of these communities not possible otherwise . . . Year after year our federation has urged tne fullest measure of support.
The Canadian citizenship council said:
Perhaps no single agency during the past ten years, with the possible exception of the C.B.C. has done more to acquaint Canadians with our great national heritage . . . The N.F.B. unhampered as commercial producers often are with the need of selling something else, has been able to sell Canada to the Canadian people.
The Ontario association of film councils said:
We owe a great debt of gratitude to the officers and field representatives of the N.F.B.
Here are the people of Canada speaking. Those are the people who apparently needed reassuring. And so it goes on. I have a quotation here from the Canadian Congress of Labour. It states:
By any standard, tne film board's achievements have been outstanding. In the circumstances they are something of a miracle.
Hence it is obvious that it was not public confidence that needed to be restored. What was needed was a little bit more backbone in government policies of the day. However, a new commissioner was appointed and he inherited a rather serry mess. I suppose there were several policies he could have followed if he had wanted to do so; but apparently, if one can judge from the films

which have been quite good-which have come out of the film board in the last few years, he
558	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. A. Stewart decided the best thing to do was to make the films as non-controversial as was humanly possible. It may have been a very good policy for these last few years, but it is not a policy which will always give the fullest vent to creative artists. One can only hope that such policy will be broadened in future.
It is fortunate that during those years the then commissioner had the wisdom to realize that they had on the staff of the film board a man who was at once an asset and an adornment to film making, no matter where it may take place. I refer to Norman McLaren, who has done some really extraordinary work in the medium of films and sound. One film which he made was called "Neighbours" which I suppose many hon. members of the house have seen, inasmuch as it has been shown on more than one occasion on Tuesday night in the railway committee room. This little film was a pleasure to see, yet apparently it was the consensus that it was not a commercial proposition, and it did not get any great showing in Canada. But it was taken off the shelves and sent down to the United States where it was entered in a competition where, mirabile dictu, it received an Oscar. I am not sure whether it received the Oscar because the name Norman McLaren was there or for the content; possibly it was for the first reason.
Now once again we have a new commissioner who inherits new problems. He is a man who is talented, cultured, and who knows Canada; and he is going to have a great chance to do what the film board was designed to do, namely to interpret Canada to Canadians. Yet the board is still subject to the assaults of a certain group in this country. Just before leaving Winnipeg I read the columns of the Winnipeg Free Press. This paper has got to the position where anything left of reactionary has to be opposed automatically. In Winnipeg we call the disease Siftonitis. But I can assure the commissioner that he will be perfectly safe if he ignores the Free Press, because I do not think it carries any great weight in debates such as this one; nor indeed can it make any very serious contribution.
Amongst other things the commissioner inherited was the vexing problem of the move to Montreal. It has been decided, and that is all there is to it. I do not for a moment question the good faith of the government in deciding to move it to Montreal. I may perhaps think it is wrong; but even on that point I am uncertain in my own mind. The other day the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) suggested that the government might like to do a double-take on the matter and reconsider the advisability of the move. But if the government has made up its mind
[Mr. Stewart (Winnipeg North) .1

I am prepared to go along with it, especially since the board itself recommended this move. But certain arguments were raised-and they were spurious arguments-supporting the move to Montreal.
We ought to be clear in our minds why this is being done. We are being told that the national film board is being removed from the deadly atmosphere of civil service bureaucracy. I have been in Ottawa off and on for some eight years, and I have not noticed that the atmosphere here is any more deadly than it is in any other area. As a matter of fact it is obviously not an argument which the government can use because, over the last seventeen years, the civil service has become largely the creation of the government; and they could scarcely accuse the civil service of causing such atmosphere. As I say, the government would be the last to use such an argument, but others have been taking it up. It is one which I do not think has any validity whatsoever, because there can be as much competent, constructive thinking going on in Ottawa as in any other part of the country.
Another argument is that we should take the national film board into the main stream of film production. Those who advance this point forget that although Ottawa is the headquarters of the national film board today it has not been the headquarters for film production, in the sense that all that was done here was the necessary research work to start off with and the editing at the end. The films have always been taken on location. Groups have been sent out, cameramen, technicians and so on, to all parts of Canada to take films and they have been, as I said, shot in large measure outside this city.
That also disposes of the argument that one has to go to Montreal or Toronto to get accomplished actors. What the film board has done in its wisdom is to use ordinary Canadians all over the country as its actors, and they have done a very good job.
Another argument that has been advanced is that the headquarters ought to be moved because of the exigencies and the needs of television. There again I would be tempted to disagree. In the first place I hope it is not the intention of the government to make the national film board just another subsidiary of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. That of course would be fatal to everything for which the film board stands. It should not tolerate it, and I do not think the C.B.C. would want to do it. We have two invaluable agencies here which if they co-operate can do immense good for Canada.
One aspect of television is that if the film board is compelled to do too much work for

the television end of the C.B.C. the chances are that those who are engaged in such work will lose their creative impulse, for this reason. They will be working toward a deadline; they will be working more in the sense of reporters rather than creative and artistic camera people, directors, producers and so on. The demands of the moment should not be allowed to obscure the real job the film board has to do, to interpret Canada to Canadians.
I do not for a moment deny the important part the film board can play in conjunction with the C.B.C. I do not deny that the film board can do an extraordinarily good job of explaining Canada to Canadians via the C.B.C.; but the film board must never forget, nor must the government, that there are rural circuits in Canada which are tremendously important. There are thousands of people living in rural areas who have no chance to see films other than through the efforts of the film board. These circuits must be maintained and films must be continued for such people.
Another argument I have heard raised is that Ottawa is off the main television stream, and therefore it would be advisable to shift the film board to the centre of that stream. That again is merely arguing that the film board should become a subsidiary of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, with which we in this group would disagree. But aside from that, if the film board were kept here surely it is not beyond the bounds of possibility that the local station, CBOT, could become a point of emanation; and if that is not possible it takes no great skill these days to send films either to Montreal or Toronto, wherever they are wanted.
Another argument, of course, is that by moving to Montreal there will be all the benefits of a central location. There is much to be said for that. The film board has been greatly handicapped in this city because it has been working in six, seven, even ten different locations at one time, and how they were ever able to do efficient work is completely beyond my comprehension. Apparently the board is now going to be reduced to two locations, one a technical producing plant in Montreal, and the other half kept here. That at least will be a great improvement, although I still wonder why the whole operation could not be kept more or less under one roof.
There have been other objections. There was one from the city of Ottawa not very long ago which struck me as being slightly hysterical, at least in typography if not in tone. The city fathers, and here I suppose I speak in a hermaphroditical sense, opposed the moving of the film board to Montreal,
The Address-Mr. Byrne but I think the basis of their opposition was not any fear of what was going to happen to the film board or any concern for it but the fact that Ottawa was going to lose a certain amount in taxes owing to the transfer of staff workers. It was not a case which impressed me very strongly. From the point of view of the film board itself the main objection probably is that removal may deprive the film board of its principal source of what can be called inspiration and information. But again that argument may not be altogether valid if a substantial part of the film board is going to be kept in this city under the commissioner.
The film board obviously must have ready access to facts, and those facts are more easily obtainable in Ottawa than anywhere else. It has to have reasonable access to those various contacts which it needs and which are here ready made. It has to have reasonable access, quick access indeed, to information it may want, and it could conceivably find Ottawa as good a source of inspiration as any other city. But as I say the die has been cast. The government has decided that the move is to be made and we accept it, although we shall watch with a very careful eye to see what is going on.
One thing I should like to impress on the house is that I do not want to see any more sniping by cabinet ministers against the film board. It is not right and it is not fair. I do not want to see the lethargy of government hamstringing the film board as has been the case in the past. Here we have a great creative agency designed to interpret Canada to Canadians and to the rest of the world. It is an agency which should be used much more than it has been in the past. I hope the board will go ahead with its avowed purpose in mind, with courage, conviction and imagination to carry out its job, and I hope above all that the government will have the good common sense to allow the board to do so.

(Mr. Fairey) to the federal government to increase its proportion of payments toward the construction of the trans-Canada highway. It is true that to build a highway through the mountains is much more difficult than crossing either the preCambrian shield or the prairie provinces. It is for this reason that I feel it should be possible to work out some sort of ratio whereby we might obtain greater assistance. It was pointed out by the hon. member for Victoria that certain sections of the highway through the mountains will cost almost $1 million a mile. I believe that in the coming year the federal government should plan to spend between $8 million and $10 million on that section of road to provide a hard-surfaced highway from Calgary to Golden, which is about 18 miles from the Yoho park boundary.
The difficult section of the trans-Canada highway through the Kicking Horse pass area will have been completed by 1954, as a result of the joint effort of the federal and provincial governments. When the sections I have mentioned are finished, they will complete what is commonly known as the triangle tour. It would not be entirely complete, but only a short stretch of provincial highway running north and south would remain to be completed. This would make one of the finest tours in Canada, having the finest scenery and tourist attractions. Already the best of motels in the western Canadian fashion have been established.
