There is a matter which I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), but in his absence I would draw it to the attention of the entire cabinet. There has been a general request for the extension of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act into British Columbia. Merely because it is called the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act does not necessarily mean the provisions of the act should not extend beyond the Rocky mountains. Is there any


particular reason why prairie farms should have any special consideration? Some farms in British Columbia are just as much in need of rehabilitation, either in the way of drainage or irrigation. In my opinion it is discriminatory to limit the scope of this act and not to include the four western provinces.
During the course of this debate we have heard that the lumbering industry in British Columbia is in some difficulty. Today my riding is particularly affected because there is a strike in progress at that point. It may not be appropriate to speak on this question in this house, because it seems there is little we can do about it. However, the fact that it is mentioned and that we are asking the parties to get together and come to some amicable agreement might be of assistance. Quite apart from the strike situation, there is a recession in the industry in that markets are not too good. Market conditions will not improve a great deal until more of the wheat in the prairie provinces has been marketed.
Be that as it may, among the outstanding issues at the present time is one which I feel is not economic and which should be played down by the operators rather than played up, as it is. That is the question of union security. I had a number of discussions on this matter before coming east, and I cannot understand the argument of the operators that if a union is a good union it need not force any individual to participate in the cost of carrying on that organization as a bargaining unit. The operators admit that a union is necessary. They want to deal with a bargaining unit, and not with individual members. In spite of this they do not wish to provide in an agreement with the union the necessary security for the union to carry on these negotiations.
As a Liberal I agree, as I know many other people do, that the Liberal party is a good party and that they are managing the affairs of Canada in a proper manner. However, I have no doubt in the world that if the payment of taxes for carrying on this administration were to be put on an entirely voluntary basis, every one of us would have to go home tomorrow for lack of expense money. This administration would collapse. When the operators agree that this is a good organization, and they accept it, why can they not go a step farther and give the union the security it requires? In the west we have more progressive labour legislation than you have in the east. In British Columbia we do have the voluntary revocable check-off by law. I do not intend to touch on the question of the gold strike in Ontario, but it is regrettable that its issues hang almost

entirely on the minimum of union security, and that is the voluntary revocable check-off.
There is another grave situation in British Columbia industry, and one of prime importance in my riding. It concerns the lead and zinc mines. Many mines in British Columbia have been forced to curtail their operations, and some have closed down entirely. It is my earnest hope that progress will be made, and I believe is being made, against the proposed imposition of a tariff by the United States. I believe we are in a more favourable position than we were last spring, in that there is not the same danger this tariff will be imposed. I would ask the government, however, to maintain close vigilance, and not to forget that the resolution I introduced on this subject last spring received some support from the government benches. I would hope it is the intention of the government, should this tariff be imposed, to immediately introduce retaliatory measures.
In so far as the lead and zinc industry affects my riding, the largest operation there is the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. They also have an auxiliary industry, namely the fertilizer industry. At the present time it is working on a full-time basis, whereas the mines and the mill are not. On November 20 the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson) made some statements with regard to fertilizer that I fear may have some effect on the marketing of our product and may lead the consumer, that is the farmer, to believe that he is being gouged. This may adversely affect the product being sold, which is now a very important industry in both East and West Kootenay owing to its stabilizing effect. Everyone is working on a full-time basis, and we should be disappointed to find that our markets are adversely affected by this adverse publicity or in any other way.
In referring to the Alberta nitrogen plant, which was taken over by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company following the last war, the hon. member had this to say, as reported at page 208 of Hansard:
As the war came to an end, this commodity began to pile up in the Calgary plant-
He was referring to the ammonium nitrates produced by the Alberta nitrogen plant. He went on to say:
-so the government developed a process whereby it could be used in the manufacture of fertilizer.
So far that is a correct picture of the situation. However, the story of Alberta nitrogen is just this. When the war broke out the technical staff of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company were loaned to the government to develop this plant and run it;
The Address-Mr. Byrne and of course it was run on a non-fee basis. The understanding was that at the end of the war, when industry would again revert to the hands of private enterprise, the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company would have the first refusal of this plant. That is, they would meet the highest offer of anyone bidding for this operation. I have said that it was Consolidated's technicians. It is true they were paid by the federal government, but they developed the process whereby the ammonium used in ammunition could be converted into fertilizer for peacetime use. It was patented, and the patent also reverted to the federal government.
The hon. member went further and said:
In spite of the fact that the federation of agriculture over and over again insisted that the government maintain that plant for the use of the farmers of Canada, they sold it to the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company in Trail, the only monopoly in the fertilizer industry, as far as we are concerned, in western Canada.
Well, as I have said, the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company bought this property on a competitive bid basis. It may be said that they have a monopoly in fertilizer in western Canada. I personally have bought fertilizer right in the town of Kimberley which was made by other companies. The fertilizer plant of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company is established in Kimberley, and there they have a large operation. Other fertilizer companies have attempted to get into the market on the prairie provinces, but they just have not been successful; they have been unable to compete in that market, and they have not been able to develop, as has been done by the technicians of Consolidated, the type of fertilizer that will give the results that are given by the fertilizer produced by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company.
To show that the hon. member is entirely confused in his statements I wish to point out that the fertilizer produced at the Alberta nitrogen plant, to which he referred, has practically no market on the western prairies. All that fertilizer, known as Nitro Prills, is exported to the United States; so when he says that a plant at Calgary was taken from the people and given to a private monopoly, and the monopoly was allowed to gouge the farmers, he is completely incorrect.
The fertilizer used in the prairie provinces is produced at Trail, British Columbia; and because of the demand on the prairies for this type of sulphur ammonia an additional plant was built at Kimberley at a cost of approximately $10 million. If the market continues to expand as it has done in the past-and it has expanded a great deal from 28,000 tons in 1942 to some 113,000 tons last year-and if

The Address-Mr. Byrne we do not get too involved by the arguments presented by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort, then the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company intends to build further units, perhaps two or three units, which will provide employment for some 150 to 200 men per unit.
There are more interesting figures relating to the use of this fertilizer on the prairie provinces, and its cost. As a union officer I had considerable discussion with the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company on the taking over of the Alberta nitrogen plant and the manner in which they operated it. As we bargained jointly, bargained for the mine, the smelter and Alberta nitrogen, I became somewhat familiar with the matter. When the hon. member spoke I made it my business to get the figures to correct some of the statements he had made.
The hon. member implies that the farmers are being gouged. I want to quote these figures. From 1935 to 1939 the price range was such that 90 bushels of wheat would purchase one ton of fertilizer. In 1951 and 1952, with the price ranges in existence at that time, it required only 65 bushels of wheat to purchase a ton of fertilizer. Not only the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson) but other hon. members on that side of the house seemed inclined to distort the picture regardless of the consequences to the industry and those people who are employed directly in the industry. The interests of the employees of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company have a direct relationship to the interests of the company itself. It is for that reason that I make these corrections.
The hon. member has stated that from the summer of 1946 the cost of production under private enterprise rose from $19 a ton to $40.59 a ton, and that it has been going up steadily ever since. I have been unable to discover where the hon. member obtained those production figures, because I have been unable to find similar figures. But let us assume for a moment that they are correct. In 1946 I recall that the wage rate at Consolidated was almost half what it was in 1952. I refer now to the basic wage scale. Perhaps my hon. friend has noted a recent statement by the dominion bureau of statistics which indicates that the highest average personal earnings of all cities in Canada are those of Trail and Kimberley. The people of those communities are mainly employed by this company. I am happy to say that up until 1949 I had considerable to do with bringing about such conditions.
While wages do not make up all the costs of production, they do have some bearing upon it. But the fact remains, as I have 
pointed out, that it takes only 65 bushels of wheat to buy a ton of fertilizer at the present time. Notwithstanding the hon. member's statement, if this matter can be cleared up to the satisfaction of those who will become new users, if they can be given the actual facts, we may expect this picture to continue. I do not believe that the convertibility or acceptance of sterling is the answer to our trade problems at the present time. I do not want to refer to provincial matters, but Social Credit members opposite have brought provincial matters into the discussion from time to time and have endeavoured to convince the house that because they have Social Credit in Alberta and because they now have it in British Columbia, everything is going to work out to the best interests of everyone.
A few moments ago I said that our basic industries of mining and lumbering were facing difficulties. Mr. Speaker, at the risk of boring the house, I wish to associate myself with the hon. members who spoke before me to offer you a personal tribute on the occasion of your election to the office of Speaker. I am one of those who are fortunate enough to have known you for the last four years and to have seen you discharge your duties in this house; without any doubt, you will do more honour to your duties than you will be honoured by them.
I wish also to congratulate the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Lesage) upon the confidence which the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has reposed in him. I may assure the hon. minister as an independent member in this house, quite secure from the excitement which is sometimes caused by partisan enthusiasm, that the people of Quebec as a whole were very happy when they heard of his appointment.
The hon. member's reputation had long since spread beyond the walls of this house, and nobody was surprised to learn that he had been promoted to a key position.
As far as I am concerned, as an impartial observer, I think that the new minister has a great opportunity to become the leading light from Quebec in the federal Liberal party within a few years. I wish it to be well understood, Mr. Speaker, that this tribute I am paying here, humble though it may be, is not mere flattery. On the contrary, I am applying here a principle which I hold very dear, that is to say that we should pay close attention to the actions of public figures, in order to criticize them when they go astray or to encourage and support them when they show themselves worthy of our trust.
I have no intention of speaking at length. I only wish, today, to make a few brief remarks on two points in particular, first the question of bilingual cheques and, secondly, the position of farmers.

On several occasions, during former sessions, I urged the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to see to it that all cheques issued by the federal government be printed in both languages. I also asked the government to do likewise for all printed matter emanating from its services. Besides, I admit that I was not the only one to do so. I realize, however, that the reaction was slow. And yet, was it not last year that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) said that such a thing was possible, when he referred to family allowance cheques? Is it not a fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) told the Conseil de Liaison Frangaise last spring that there was no objection to that? So then, what are we waiting for? In the hope that the claimants will get tired of asking? On this point, let no one misunderstand what I say: as long as I am entitled, with others, to speak in this house, such a thing will not happen.
Are we opposed to bilingualism with respect to coins, paper money and stamps? Apparently, the practical application of the principle of bilingualism has not been harmful, from a strictly electoral viewpoint, to the Liberal party.
This condition I am talking about creates the definite impression that the French Canadians living outside Quebec are in an exclusively English country, while those of us who live in Quebec should be thankful that we are permitted to live in some sort of reservation, which is tolerated, in the very heart of an English country.
Several months have already passed since the Minister of Finance stated that cheques would soon be bilingual in the province of Quebec and even, conditions permitting, across Canada. I for one was not satisfied with that answer.
However that statement received much publicity throughout the country, not only in French newspapers but in English newspapers as well. We have had a general election since then, and it does not appear that such a statement of policy did any harm to the Liberal party.
Several months have gone by since then, but nothing has been done, even as far as Quebec province is concerned. And if it takes that long to carry out that promise in the province of Quebec, how long will it take to carry it out across the country?

I have said it already but I wish to repeat it once more: we are much more broadminded in the province of Quebec. Whatever their affiliation, our political leaders are broadminded enough to show their faith in bilingualism by printing, in both languages, all the official documents. And yet scarcely more than 12 per cent of the people under their jurisdiction are English-speaking, while, on the federal plane, the French-speaking minority represents more than 30 per cent of the total population. We see, then, that those 30 per cent are unable to obtain from our Canadian statesmen what our leaders in Quebec are generous enough to grant to 12 per cent of Quebec's population.
Where is that spirit of understanding, of justice, and of good will we hear so much about? Have we ever heard the majority in Quebec protest against the off-handed manner in which the leaders, of whatever party they may be, treat the minority?
In the federal field, I am ready to put my confidence in the good sense and the fair play of the Canadian element of English origin, the most important ethnic group in the country, and I am sure that they will be just as well disposed toward the French minority in Canada as we are toward the English minority in Quebec.
In the debate which will follow the presentation of the budget, I intend to urge the government to grant some assistance to our poorer citizens and to our large families. I shall very likely get the answer which was given a few times in the past four years: where will you get the money needed to put your plan in operation? In the present case, it might be my turn to ask the question: How much will the treasury have to disburse to grant my request? And if nobody answers me I shall be compelled to reply myself: not one cent. Where are the objections?
I understand that when some members, myself included, request a national flag for Canada, a national anthem or a representative to the Vatican, it can always be said, and quite improperly in my opinion, that the time has not come yet, that public opinion is not ripe, that unity has not been attained in regard to such matters. Those are debatable matters to say the least. But as far as bilingualism on cheques and other documents is concerned, who are the ones that object?

The Address-Mr. Poulin Where are they? Where and when have they protested and in whose name or on whose behalf?
Those are some of the things that we should like to learn, to enable us to understand why no action has yet been taken on the matter although two ministers have stated that it could be done.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to be unpleasant, nor do I wish to impute motives to anyone. Let us simply say, for now, that those who could correct the situation have not yet realized the full importance of the problem and the inconsequence of the present situation. It might be good for them, however, to hurry, because the time might soon come where an important part of our population will accuse them of discrimination and lack of good will.
Dealing now with the second point-and that is the last question I shall bring up-I notice that the speech from the throne has very little to say about the situation of agriculture in Canada. I will quote verbatim everything that concerns that important part of our economy. I quote Hansard of November 12, 1953, page 5:
Our farmers have harvested the second largest wheat crop in Canadian history . . .
A bill to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act to provide for appropriate compensation to farmers whose hogs suffered from cholera, will he placed before you.
It must be recognized that this announcement does not go too far.
Like everybody else, I am, of course, happy to learn that the farmers of the western provinces have benefited from a very abundant harvest this fall. That means prosperity for most of them. Unfortunately, I cannot be equally optimistic in respect of the present situation of our eastern farmers. I refer especially to those who specialize in the breeding of beef cattle.
We all know that the dairy industry is the main interest of the farmers of Ontario and Quebec. Along with that-and directly because of it-the same farmers are also deeply interested in the breeding of beef cattle. They either fatten and sell as they are the young animals they consider useless for the maintenance of their dairy herds, or they sell the dairy cows themselves, when they no longer give enough milk. I would go so far as to say that in a number of cases their income from that source equals or exceeds the income resulting from the sale of dairy products. It is consequently quite in order to say that the situation of the dairy producer, in eastern Canada, is jeopardized with every fall in the price or market for livestock.

Now, what is the situation today in this respect? Overnight, at the beginning of 1952, the price for cattle paid to the farmer fell to an excessively low level. Cattle which were selling for $175 or $200 a head in 1951 are selling this year for $40 or $50 a head, and it is not always easy to find a buyer at that price.
Last autumn, I travelled about the county of Beauce and several other parts of Quebec. I was particularly impressed by the grazing herds; they seemed to grow at both ends, if I may use that expression; I mean that contrary to what is usual at this time of the year, we notice, on the one hand, a great number of fatted calves and, on the other, some old cattle that are also fat and ready for the packing-plant, but not yet sold.
The farmer will lose this revenue and, what is more, he will have to keep these animals in the stalls all winter long, without much hope of disposing of them at a better price next year.
Moreover, all those things the farmer needs to maintain his herd are still too expensive; I shall only mention meals. The farmer is thus, from both viewpoints, in a very critical position, and it is hardly possible to foresee any improvement in the situation, if we let our economy take its course in the hope that everything will come out all right.
This situation looks so serious to me that I am wondering whether the government should not try to do something, without interfering with the sacred principle of free competition and private enterprise? There surely comes a time when the latter is no longer able to serve public interest, when the mechanism of private enterprise, probably because of the mistakes of certain interested parties, does not function properly within our liberal economic system.
Perhaps someone will object that the American market, which much too often gives the lead to ours, is faced with the same difficulties. However I do not see in this fact any reason not to attempt to do something to correct a situation which has become very precarious. I do not admit that the prices on our markets should be based on the prices on the United States markets. There is no more reason for it in this case than in the case, for example, of automobiles and electrical appliances, which are sold much cheaper in the United States.
I do not think the government is to blame for this. However, I do think that they should try and find some means to remedy the state of affairs which I have just described and about which the least that can be said is that

it is certainly very serious for the farmers in my riding.
There is another side to the problem, about which I would like to make known the viewpoint of those I have the privilege of representing here. It is the astounding discrepancy which exists between the price received by the producer and the price paid at the consumer level by those who buy their meat from the retailer. The worker and the low wage earner, who eke out a bare existence since the new rise in the cost of living, still pay practically the same price for their meat as they did when cattle prices were very high. The facts seem to contradict the situation described to us in the House of Commons on Monday, November 30, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), when he said: "From now on the seller's market is going to become a buyer's market." I believe that in this case it is not a seller's market nor a buyer's market, but rather a middleman's market, that of the Canada Packers, the Swift Canadian or the Legrade Incorporated.
If what we hear is true, it would seem that our neighbours to the south have authorized a government investigation into similar conditions over there.
If things do not get better here, it would undoubtedly be advisable for our government to do likewise to put an end to this shameless exploitation of our workers and wage earners in our cities and towns, who are practically defenceless against callous people who only seek to reap large profits.
Mr. Speaker, if I did not fear to prolong unduly this debate I would call the attention of the house to some of the proposals contained in the speech from the throne which forecast excellent government legislation.
I could mention, among other things, the bills to help the disabled persons and to amend the National Housing Act. However, it would probably be wiser to wait and see whether our hopes will be fulfilled.
Moreover, there are on the government side excellent speakers who succeeded in bringing out everything worth while in that document, so that I could add nothing that has not already been said.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first may I join my colleagues on all sides of this house in extending my con-
The Address-Mr. Nickle gratulations on your elevation to your new high office. I am sure that you, as have your distinguished predecessors, will add honour and dignity to the house and bring new distinction to yourself.
Throughout this house, except perhaps among a small group who pin their hopes on state control or state ownership of everything, there is general agreement or general acceptance of the principles involved in the amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Because I wish to devote my remarks today to the support of those principles, let me briefly recite the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), and seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green):
We respectfully represent to Your Excellency that the welfare of Canada is dependent upon free competition; and that the prosperity and security of all Canadians will be advanced by government policies which will restore markets for primary products and generally promote a high volume of international trade.
With my colleagues of course I strongly support that amendment.
Much has already been said in this debate about Canada's agricultural industry and its problems, problems which are of vital concern to the west where grain and livestock, and the volume of production, saleability and price of grain and livestock, largely determine the state of economic health of the entire west, and indeed also materially affect the economic health of Canada. My purpose today, however, is not to discuss agriculture. Hon. members who know far more about this subject than I are doing that. I merely wish to emphasize one point, namely that western Canada today is too dependent for its economic health upon this single industry. The building up of a diversified economy in the west is vital to the security of the people there.
Like the maritimes, the west needs what Ontario and Quebec already possess, namely diversified industry. We need in the west, as indeed we do in all Canada, greater freedom of enterprise and the incentive that encourages the speed-up of our national building. We need freedom for growth, the right to sell our products with the absolute minimum of restrictions in the markets both Canadian and foreign; and I also mean, of course, with full awareness that trade must be a two-way deal.
We need people, many more millions of people in our west and elsewhere across this country to provide human resources for our development and greater human markets for

The Address-Mr. Nickle our own products. But expanded immigration, Mr. Speaker, must go hand in hand with basic resources and industrial expansion. We need capital; we need many billions of dollars. We must offer the incentive of freedom, fair dealing and possible profit to continue getting capital in the required amounts from Canadians as well as from the United States, Great Britain and other lands.
We western Canadians, perhaps to a greater degree than those elsewhere in our country, realize the importance of breaking down the barriers to international trade. Without export markets our agricultural industry upon which the western economy is now so dependent, would die and carry the west into the grave with it. Those export markets will continue to expand on a healthy basis only if our overseas customers can earn dollars through the sale of their products to North America with which to pay for our wheat, cattle, apples, cheese and other products. Particularly important in this regard are the motherland islands of our British commonwealth.
We western Canadians also realize, perhaps to a greater extent than easterners, the vital importance to our economy of increasing co-operation with our neighbour to the south in the mutual breaking down of trade and tariff and other kinds of barriers between our two great nations of North America. The industrial future of Alberta, British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, based for example on their hydrocarbons-coal, oil, gas and by-products-will be shaped to a very considerable degree by the extent of freedom of movement of those products over the Canadian-United States border and the extent to which our two nations accept the economically sound integration of mineral resources on a continental rather than a national basis.
It is these hydrocarbon resources, which have been found by free enterprise in steadily increasing amounts in the vast regions from the Rocky mountains to Manitoba, that provide western Canada with the greatest opportunity in our history to build a diversified economy of industries to supplement the present mighty agriculture.
On the broad questions of greater freedom of trade and free enterprise there have been some important statements in recent weeks. The speech from the throne delivered by His Excellency the Governor General had this to say for Canada's present government:
My ministers are convinced that nations can best achieve economic strength and security through more liberal trade and overseas investment policies and they are continuing their efforts to bring about the progressive reduction of trade restrictions.

I recall the words of President Dwight Eisenhower when he addressed this parliament on November 14. Let me quote what he said:
The free world must come to recognize that trade barriers, although intended to protect a country's economy, often in fact shackle its prosperity. In the United States there is a growing recognition that free nations cannot expand their productivity and economic strength without a high level of international trade.
An outstanding Canadian, Donald Gordon, president of the Canadian National Railways, had some common-sense things to say about trade barriers, economic nationalism and free enterprise when he addressed the bankers' club of Detroit a week or so ago. Let me quote a few of his words:
Free enterprise means to me not freedom from competition, but rather freedom to enter into competition; to buy and sell in any market at the best price as determined by natural economic forces operating in a framework of fair opportunity.
This government slammed the doors against competition by Canadian Pacific Air Lines with the government monopoly, Trans-Canada Air Lines, in the field of air cargo transport, but it might have taken different action had it listened to such stirring words by Mr. Gordon:
Free enterprise means not freedom from competition, but rather freedom to enter into competition.
In days ahead, when weighing decisions on other matters now pending, I trust this government will remember also another key statement by Mr. Gordon:
I am profoundly convinced that any policy attempted along the lines of economic nationalism, or falling short of an all-out effort towards clearing away all impediments to the international exchange of goods and services . . . will not only work against the interests of the United States and Canada, but may well be calamitous to the kind of world we would like to live in.
The chief of my party, the Leader of the Opposition in this house, made an important restatement of Conservative party policy on November 16 when he pledged my party to all-out support of free enterprise. I am in firm agreement with such words of his as these:
Freedom within the law is that right of every citizen of Canada, and as an individual, or jointly with others, he has the right to set up a new business, engage in a new type of production, or venture into new fields with a possibility of reward which offers some return for the risks he takes. Success brings increased employment and prosperity for all.
Nothing else has yet been discovered which provides the incentive upon which an expanding economy can be built. This is no time to be limiting expansion in this young country of ours. Years ago we found that even with all our

resources, restrictive practices could prove disastrous to Canadian workers. Let us take no chance of repeating that mistake.
Through the years there has been a tendency in Canada, as well as in other nations, to bring government increasingly into business, a tendency due in part to actions and attitudes of business, politicians and the public in other nations, as well as actions and attitudes of business, politicians and the public in our own Canada. More and more has government been getting into business, granting or expanding direct subsidies to some industries, extending indirect subsidies through such means as tariff barriers to other industries, and also in some instances going directly into business, sometimes as a government monopoly.
I am, on principle, against government in business, and against subsidies direct or indirect to industries. So probably are most Canadians, who as taxpayers have to foot the bill. However, it is a bit like sin- most everybody is "agin" it. But we must accept the fact that sin, like government in business, subsidies and tariffs, is with us. Nevertheless I firmly believe that the less we have of these things, the better off Canada and the world will be.
I believe the great majority of Canadians recognize that subsidized industries-whether by direct subsidies, tariff supports or other aids -are in some degree sick industries. As with sick humans, we nurse them; but the sooner they can stand on their own feet and fight their own battles of life without nursing, the better off they and we will be.
While there are obvious immediate benefits from government nursing for those working in or dependent upon subsidized industries, we must also consider the great drawbacks. First, there is the cost to the economy as a whole and the burden upon Canadians generally, of the nursing care, the direct and indirect subsidies, and the higher cost of goods behind a tariff wall. Second, there is the tendency of sick industries to sicken healthy industries around them, and for the demands for nursing care to pyramid. Third, there is the tendency of tariffs and other barriers to international trade to pyramid between nations, thus weakening industries whose major markets must be found beyond their national borders and creating new barriers and misunderstandings between nations.
I believe it is the responsibility of this and succeeding governments, this and succeeding parliaments, and also the responsibility of Canada's taxpaying public and of Canada's industries and business leaders, to resist the trend toward what sometimes
The Address-Mr. Nickle seems the easiest and politically expedient way out of a problem, subsidies of one form or another.
In my own words, and with quotes from statements of others, I have outlined the general principles guiding my thinking on industrial development, freedom of enterprise and trade policies for Canada. Let us briefly apply those principles to some phases of the new industrial hopes for western Canada.
Recent years have brought proof beyond doubt that our west is a vast treasure-house of crude oil, natural gas and the associated by-products of sulphur and liquid hydrocarbon. Free enterprise, made up of hundreds of companies Canadian and foreign, has already proved up some 2,000 million barrels of oil, over 14,000 billion cubic feet of gas, and many millions of tons of associated by-products, worth in all over $5 billion.
The important fact is not the measure of reserves proved to date, but the growing proof that reserves many times greater than those known today are still hidden below the ground waiting for discovery. The rate of discovery, and the rate of increase in value of those resources to the west and Canada, depend upon incentive.
The best incentive is freedom to grow and the right to sell into the most economic markets at the best possible prices. The alternative to such freedom, if this western industry is to grow, is subsidized nationalism. The geography of North America, and the population and market distribution over North America, leave no other alternative. The west's oil and gas fields and its petrochemical plants of the future, are a long cost-distance removed from Canada's major market, Ontario and Quebec. Much closer and more economic are markets in the neighbouring United States, provided Canada and the United States do not erect a border barrier. By effective international co-operation now and in the future the west's great new resources can grow by stages, on a sound basis, to ensure a long-term supply of hydrocarbons for Canada, a supplementary supply for our neighbour, and a strengthened Canadian economy.
In Quebec and Labrador vast iron ore deposits have been uncovered, and hundreds of millions of dollars are being spent to develop these deposits and provide a railway link to the St. Lawrence, opening doors to markets. This great project is only possible now because of the freedom provided to ship a high percentage of the ore to our hungry neighbour, the United States.
If we took the stand that Labrador ore, together with the iron deposits being developed at Steep Rock and in western Ontario,

The Address-Mr. Nickle must be held in Canada for our possible future needs, the great projects now developing would be seriously restricted, perhaps even killed. Instead, we are following the common-sense plan of selling ore to foreign markets in order to ensure development of Canadian reserves, the resultant expansion of Canadian markets for steel, the expansion of Canadian plants for the processing of ores, and speeding the discovery rate of new Canadian reserves, thereby looking after Canada's future in this regard.
The same common-sense principles apply in regard to our other base metals, zinc, lead, copper and so on. What would happen to the important base metal mining and smelting industries in British Columbia, the prairies, central Canada and the maritimes if we closed the door to exports on the ground that the reserves should be held for Canada's possible needs, sometime in the long-term future?
Consider the vast aluminum industry of Quebec and the great new aluminum plant at Kitimat, created by mating low-cost Canadian hydroelectric energy with bauxite imported from South America and the West Indies. These vital Canadian industries would sicken and decline if the bauxite-producing countries barred export on the grounds that the processing should be done in the country of origin, or that the bauxite should be held for their own future needs. Our Canadian aluminum industry would also slump should the doors to foreign markets for its surplus be slammed shut.
If we are to bar the door to export for one or two of our natural resources on the grounds they may be needed sometime in the distant future to serve our own needs, why not extend the same argument to all our resources, for example, the products of our vast pulp and paper and lumbering industries, our iron ore and other base metals, and so on down the list?
No, Mr. Speaker. With oil and gas and their by-products, as well as with all Canada's treasure-house of resources, their discovery and development and the extent of their contribution to Canada's growth and economic health, depend upon incentive and freedom to market at fair prices, with the prospect of fair return.

All engineering and geological authorities on western Canada's oil and gas resources, including the top authorities in the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and dominion geological survey, now agree that the west's ultimate reserves will be many times those known today, if incentive to discover continues. In other words we are going to have oil, gas and by-products adequate for all Canadian markets, plus the United States markets within economic reach, for far more years than we need worry about. Then ultimately, when demand outstrips the supply of natural oil and gas, Alberta's tar sands and coal deposits will provide the means for liquid and gaseous hydrocarbons for many more hundreds of years.
Why not, therefore, plan our marketing on the soundest basis, reaching first into the nearest and most economic markets both in Canada and the United States, then gradually reaching outward to the most distant Canadian and American markets as sound economics permit? Through effective co-operation with the United States such a program could bring United States gas into the mass market of our east, pending ultimate deliveries from western Canada. We already operate along this line in the case of oil, with foreign oil serving the eastern half of Canada's market and our own western surplus going into the nearest United States markets. If it be Canada's desire that only Canadian gas go as quickly as possible to Ontario and Quebec, markets that normally, on an economic basis, would be served by western gas in the second stage of market development, then we must pay the price-subsidies.
To all in government, to all believers in free enterprise, free competition and greater international trade, and to all opponents of too much government in business and too much business dependence upon the taxpayers who pay the bills of government, I urge careful consideration of the matters I have outlined today.
On motion of Mr. Nickle the debate was adjourned.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
